title: The Ishango bone recovered by Lake Edward
institution: Royal Belgian Institute of Natural Sciences
dateKind: The institute’s estimate for the bone and the separately documented year of excavation
observation: Recovered on the Congolese bank of Lake Edward in 1950, the roughly 10 cm bone holds a quartz fragment at one end. The museum identifies groups of three and six, four and eight, and five and ten marks on one side.
limit: Those matching counts leave the maker's purpose open. It is possible to report the numerical relationship while leaving its historical interpretation unfinished.
alt: Original pixel drawing of the thin Ishango bone, with groups of cut marks and a small angular quartz tip.
methodReply: Lella can hand runners a reliable way to reproduce the three doubles with beads. She clips a separate line to the tally so nobody has to guess what the bone's maker counted.
contextReply: Omrin leaves a blank headed ‘possible uses’ below the bone's excavation record. People can still see the doubled groups while leaving the maker’s purpose open.
market: The stall worked out twice the bundle count with the running strip. Its clerk writes ‘bundles’ beside the sum so a visitor can tell it apart from sales.

title: Plimpton 322, the Old Babylonian clay tablet at Columbia
institution: Columbia University Rare Book and Manuscript Library
dateKind: Date and Larsa attribution used by Columbia University Libraries
observation: Columbia attributes this tablet to Larsa, now Tell Senkereh in Iraq. Its cuneiform rows encode numbers in base 60. The library presents the reading of the numbers as right-triangle relations and a scholar’s interpretation that a teacher used the tablet.
limit: A numerical relation can hold for a row and leave the intended use of the broken tablet undecided.
alt: Original pixel drawing of the rectangular clay tablet. One edge is broken and there are dark ruled bands of cuneiform marks.
methodReply: Lella brings the checked triangle frames to her apprentice. He can use two example sizes before learning where each relation came from.
contextReply: Omrin leaves sight of the broken edge on the reader’s copy. He gives the surviving relationships and the proposed teaching use separate lines.
market: An apprentice copies the check for the two small triangular frames. The row on the display labels the fit as a property of the model and keeps the tablet’s possible use on its own slip.

title: Bakhshali manuscript, MS. Sansk. d. 14
date: Birch bark from three leaves dated 224–383, 680–779 and 885–993 CE
dateKind: Dates of tested birch bark. The writing date and assembly of the surviving manuscript are debated.
observation: The birch-bark leaves were found at Bakhshali, in present-day Pakistan, in 1881. The manuscript uses a dot where an empty place must remain in a number. Oxford’s report gives different age ranges for three bark samples.
limit: The date of a tested leaf and the date of its writing or assembly answer different questions. Scholars have proposed different readings of the dating evidence.
alt: Original pixel drawing of the manuscript’s thin, overlapping brown birch-bark leaves, with chipped edges and several dark lines of ink.
methodReply: Lella uses the visible gap to check that her line of tallies gives the units a place. She keeps the demonstration apart from the old page’s dates.
contextReply: Omrin can file the sample dates alongside a precise note about what was dated. He leaves a space for an account of when the lines were written.
market: A shop runner can read the three columns left by the divider. The price slip gives the empty tens place a mark so the next stall can follow the same record.
